# Introduction

The study of bacterial microbiomes has exploded over the last two decades, with hundreds of papers being made on a wide range of areas. There is always more that can be inferred due to the ubiquitous nature of bacteria. This nature forces interaction with the environments in which they live, as they and the environment adapt around each other. These interactions are important and can have practical uses. For example, microbiomes can be used to assist plants in ways ranging from growth enhancement to the alleviation of pathogen infection. Many papers have researched the impact of probiotic microbiomes on plant growth in many species. However, not all bacteria interact well or produce good results, so better knowledge of these microbiomes is vital [@compant2019].

These uses do not end at conservation, as human health depends on the interplay inside the gut. For example, bacteria digest many compounds the human body cannot and create useful amino acids and vitams [@mendes2015]. @vandeputte2017 found that subjects with Crohn's disease had significantly lower microbial loads and quantitative genus abundance, implying a link between a disrupted microbiome and the disease. @obrien2019 discuss these interactions in the context of the hologenome, how interactions can shape genomics in both the host and mutualistic symbionts. Much information on gene function can be gained through genomic study, with many methods to do so [@levy2018]. This will help illuminate these interactions and allow for the hypothesis on how microbiota can combat global challenges, as mentioned above.

This study used bottom-up estimates of function based on gene content as a genomic tool to research bacteria comprising host-associated microbiomes. Primarily, study was conducted upon 10 Genomic samples from the skin microbiome of the dying poison dart frog (*Dendrobates tinctorius*)*.* These were created by Post-graduate researchers at the ECW labs at Bangor as part of a larger project. The secondary source of data was the NCBI database. There is a massive wealth of information on the NCBI. For example, 2.61 million bacterial genomes that are public and free to utilize. This data was easily downloaded and aided analysis.

With these data sources combined, many exploratory computational experiments could be done on the data, with the aim of identifying functional differences between the samples . An emphasis was placed on how evolutionary history and host-environment can shape these genetics, building on research by [@lunjani2021]. The aims of this project are to learn more about the genomes of these samples, namely the functions of the genes therein, as well as look into the phylogenetic relationships of the samples. Secondary aims are to develop bioinformatic and general scientific skills. Such as data analysis and visualisation, as well as understand the tools used, for the purposes of future research and gain skills in genomics and bioinformatics.
